Given milk mixed with water, the Prophet passed the rest to the bedouin on his right rather than to Abu Bakr, saying to begin from the right.
The Prophet accepted and ate the thighs of a rabbit Anas caught, but declined an onager presented while he was in Ihram, explaining this to the saddened giver.
People sent gifts on Aisha's day; the Prophet ate gifts but not charity, saying charity given to Barirah was a gift for him, and left a gifted mastigar he disliked.
Um Salama's group of wives asked that gifts reach the Prophet in any wife's house; he said revelation came to him only in Aisha's bed, and Aisha silenced Zainab.
Anas, like the Prophet, would not refuse gifts of perfume.
The Prophet asked the Muslims to return the repentant Hawazin's captives as a favour or for later compensation, and they agreed willingly.
The Prophet accepted gifts and gave in return, and told a father who had given one son a slave to be just to his children and take the gift back.
In his serious illness the Prophet, with his wives' leave, was nursed in Aisha's house, walking there supported between Al-Abbas and Ali with his feet dragging.
One who takes back his gift is like a dog that swallows its vomit.
Asma, whose only property came from Az-Zubair, was told to give in charity and not withhold or give reluctantly, lest Allah withhold from her.
Maimuna was told giving her slave-girl to her maternal uncles would have earned more than freeing her; the Prophet drew lots among his wives, and Sauda gave Aisha her turn.
Asked which of two neighbours should get her gift, Aisha was told the one whose door is nearer.
The Prophet declined As-Sa'b's gift of onager meat at Al-Abwa' or Waddan because he was in Ihram, and told the saddened giver so.
A zakat collector who claimed presents given to him was asked whether he would have got them at home; whoever takes zakat unlawfully will carry it on his neck.
Abu Bakr paid Jabir what the Prophet had promised him from Bahrain's funds, and the Prophet kept a cloak aside for Makhrama from those he distributed.
A man who had intercourse while fasting in Ramadan could not free a slave, fast two months or feed sixty poor, so dates given for expiation went to his family.
When creditors harshly demanded the debt of Jabir's father, martyred at Uhud, the Prophet blessed his date-palms, and their fruit paid them in full with much left over.
Offered a drink, the Prophet asked the boy on his right to let the old men on his left drink first, but the boy would not yield his share.
The Prophet paid Jabir what he owed him and more, weighing out the price of the camel Jabir had sold him with an extra amount.
The boy on the Prophet's right refused to give up his turn to the old men on his left, so the Prophet put the bowl in his hand.
When a creditor demanded his debt harshly, the Prophet stopped his companions, saying he had the right to speak, and repaid him an older camel, as the best repay best.
Hawazin's delegation, made to choose between their property and their captives, chose the captives, and the Muslims, through their leaders, agreed willingly to return them.
Owing a camel of a certain age, the Prophet let its owner demand it and repaid him an older camel, saying the best repay their debts most handsomely.
The Prophet bought Umar's troublesome camel, which kept going ahead of him, and gave it to Abdullah bin Umar to do with as he liked.
Calling a silk cloak the dress of one with no share in the Hereafter, the Prophet sent Umar one not to wear, and Umar gave it to a pagan brother.
The Prophet would not enter Fatima's house because of a decorated curtain, saying he had no interest in worldly things, and had it sent to needy people.
Ali cut up a silk dress the Prophet gave him on seeing his anger, and of a silk cloak from Ukaidir the Prophet said Sa'd's handkerchiefs in Paradise are better.
A Jewess brought the Prophet a poisoned sheep and he ate of it; he refused to have her killed, and Anas kept seeing the poison's effect in his mouth.
With 130 companions, the Prophet bought a sheep from a pagan, gave everyone a piece of its roasted organs, and its meat filled two basins, with food left over.
The Prophet sent Umar a silk cloak not to wear but to sell or give away, and Umar sent it to his brother in Mecca, not yet a Muslim.
Asma asked whether to keep good relations with her pagan mother who had come to her, and the Prophet said yes.
Taking back a gift is like a dog swallowing its vomit, so Umar was told not to buy back, even for a dirham, a horse he gave in Allah's cause.
Asma was told to keep good relations with her polytheist mother, who came to her in the Prophet's lifetime.
The Prophet ruled that an umra belongs to the one to whom it is presented, and that it is permissible.
When Medina was alarmed, the Prophet borrowed Abu Talha's horse Al-Mandub, rode out, found nothing to fear, and praised the horse's speed.
Aisha, in a coarse five-dirham dress, says that in the Prophet's time women wishing to look elegant would borrow such a dress from her.
Lending a milch animal is a fine charity, best of forty deeds; land is better given free than rented, and the Ansar's gifted palms were returned after Khaibar.
Abraham migrated with Sarah, who was given Hajar as a slave-girl, and Sarah said Allah had humiliated the pagan.
Umar was told not to buy back a horse he had given in Allah's cause, as one should not take back what one gave in charity.
When liars accused Aisha, the Prophet consulted Ali and Usama, Barirah found no fault in her but youth, and he asked for help against the man who defamed his family.
